questions.q: Recall the three languages, besides English, that Milton read extensively after Cambridge, as mentioned in the textbook’s introductory note.
questions.a: Latin, Greek, and Italian. A wrong answer (e.g., “French, German, Spanish”) shows the student has not read the biographical note carefully and will miss the classical allusions that saturate Milton’s verse.

questions.q: Explain in your own words why the textbook describes Time as “envious” and connects it to the myth of Cronos devouring his children.
questions.a: “Envious” personifies Time as a jealous destroyer that consumes every mortal thing, just as Cronos swallowed his offspring to prevent being overthrown. A student who says “Time is just passing” misses the mythological layer that frames the poem’s central conflict between temporal decay and eternal bliss.

questions.q: Apply the concept of “Plummets” (the lead weight regulating a clock) to the line “Whose speed is but the heavy Plummets pace”. What does this image suggest about the speaker’s attitude toward measured time?
questions.a: The plummet’s slow, mechanical descent mirrors the “lazy leaden‑stepping hours” — time feels ponderous and artificial to a soul awaiting eternity. An answer that only defines “plummet” without linking it to the speaker’s impatience shows surface‑level comprehension.

questions.q: Analyse how Milton’s role as Latin Secretary (translating state papers for the Commonwealth) might inform the poem “On Shakespeare”, which praises a playwright who “needs no monument”.
questions.a: As a civil servant of the revolutionary government, Milton valued merit over hereditary pomp; similarly, he argues Shakespeare’s “easie numbers” outlive stone pyramids because they live in readers’ hearts. A response that ignores Milton’s political career fails to connect his republican ideals to his literary criticism.

questions.q: Evaluate the claim: “Milton’s blindness is the single most important biographical fact for understanding both poems in this chapter.” Defend or challenge with evidence from the text.
questions.a: Challenge: while blindness explains the dictation of *Paradise Lost*, “On Time” and “On Shakespeare” were written decades earlier (1630 and 1630s). The more crucial contexts are his classical education and Puritan worldview. A student who over‑emphasises blindness confuses the chronology and misattributes the poems’ concerns.

questions.q: Create a 4‑line stanza in Miltonic style (iambic pentameter, elevated diction) that expresses a modern student’s anxiety about board exams as a battle against “envious Time”.
questions.a: Example: “Fly, envious Hours, till answer‑scripts are done, / Call on the lagging minutes, heavy‑lead, / That crawl like plummets till the set of sun; / Our fate hangs balanced on the marks we’ve read.” A weak attempt uses simple rhyme without metre or Miltonic vocabulary, revealing unfamiliarity with his verse texture.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: "Before You Read: Context and Background" for Milton's poems provides the essential historical, ______, and literary framework needed to interpret "On Time" and "On Shakespeare" — including Milton's life (1608–1674), his blindness, his role as Latin Secretary, the turbulent politics of 17th‑century England, and the Renaissance humanist tradition that shapes his poetic voice.

Fill in the blank: Imagine you are about to watch a ______ drama set in 17th‑century England — you would want to know who the king is, what the religious conflicts are, and why the characters speak in such elevated language.
What is "Before You Read? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: "Before You Read: Context and Background" for Milton's poems provides the essential historical, biographical, and literary framework needed to interpret "On Time" and "On Shakespeare" — including Milton's life (1608–1674), his blindness, his role as Latin Secretary, the turbulent politics of 17th‑century England, and the Renaissance.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Imagine you are about to watch a historical drama set in ______th‑century England — you would want to know who the king is, what the religious conflicts are, and why the characters speak in such elevated language.
What common mix-up does this lesson flag about "Before You Read?
questions.a: Students often believe “On Shakespeare” was written *after* Milton’s blindness because they associate all Milton poems with his later dictation period.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can explain how Milton’s blindness, Puritan convictions, and classical education influence the themes of time, eternity, and poetic immortality in the two prescribed poems, and can identify at least two historical events (e.g., English Civil War, Restoration) that form the backdrop of his work.
